doc.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998

title: Imitators and James Last
summary: Conniff wasted two years with attorneys trying to stop imitators before moving on; only James Last survived by developing his own style.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Did you start to hear some imitators? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Oh yeah, there were a lot of them. As a matter of fact I wasted about two years of my life trying to find a way to stop them from doing it. And I had attorneys and copyright attorneys and regular attorneys, and we did a lot of research. We found out, they found out that I couldn’t — it’s different now, you can copyright arrangements now — well you could in those days but it was a very complicated thing I ran into. I finally found that the best thing for me to do was to forget about all the imitators, and just keep going on ahead and move ahead, and what came to me, and not worry about if someone else is imitating me. And I found out that they all fell by the wayside, it wasn’t really a — there was only one that really survived and he didn’t survive by copying. There was a fellow in Europe that became quite popular and he originally copied me when he started, but eventually he developed his own style and became — James Last — he became quite well known in Europe.
